title: MAINT: break a few circular imports
body:
#### What does this implement/fix?

The imports in `scipy.spatial.transform` are order-sensitive: sorting them alphabetically gives:

    $ python -c 'import scipy.spatial.transform'
    ImportError: cannot import name 'Rotation' from partially initialized module 'scipy.spatial.transform' (most likely due to a circular import)

The same in some other modules. The PR fixes some latent bugs related to that, mostly by importing the sibling module instead of the parent module that re-exports things from the sibling module.

#### Additional information

Checked with uncycle (`pip install uncycle`) against the parent commit:

```
$ uncycle --baseline ../parent/scipy scipy
```

body:
#### Reference issue
Towards #25964 

#### What does this implement/fix?
Corrects return dtypes for several functions and adds some tests for all functions listed in the reference issue except for `fractional_matrix_power` since that one is quite tough to properly audit. This applies for example to `clarkson_woodruff_transform` and `expm_frechet`.

#### Additional information
Some CI failures are expected:
- For `solve_toeplitz` it used to be the case that the arrays were always cast to either `float64` or `complex128`. This is now corrected to cast to `cdsz`, but does not explicitly guard against other exotic cases such as `float16`/`complex256` leading to some CI failures in `test_deprecations` since the cython code is not implemented to deal with this. Probably the best way to resolve this is to add the "normal" sequence of `_deprecate_dtypes -> _normalize_lapack_dtype` and probably adjust those tests accordingly?
- For `solve_discrete_lyapunov` I am getting some failures locally for `n=5` due to (excessively) large mismatches, but this seems to also be present on main so this might be something that warrants its own issue?

Furthermore, the testsuite for `solve_toeplitz` might now be excessively large.

title: ENH: add Wright's generalized Bessel function
body:
#### Reference issue
This function is one crucial step towards #11291. See also mailing list thread https://mail.python.org/pipermail/scipy-dev/2020-January/023918.html.

#### What does this implement/fix?
This PR adds Wright's generalized Bessel function as `scipy.special.wright_bessel`, see https://dlmf.nist.gov/10.46.E1.

#### Additional information.
~~This is a pure Python implementation that aims for correctness and not for speed.~~ I did not find any public implementation as a reference.
As it is an entire function, the series representation is always valid. ~~I tried asymptotic expansions for large argument z, without any luck.~~

Edit:
So far, only non-negative values of rho=a, beta=b and z=x are implemented. There are 5 different approaches depending on the ranges of the arguments.

1. Taylor series expansion in x=0 [1], for x <= 1.
    Involves gamma funtions in each term.
2. Taylor series expansion in x=0 [2], for large a.
3. Taylor series in a=0, for tiny a and not too large x.
4. Asymptotic expansion for large x [3, 4].
    Suitable for large x while still small a and b.
5. Integral representation [5], in principle for all arguments.


References:
- [1] https://dlmf.nist.gov/10.46.E1
- [2] P. K. Dunn, G. K. Smyth (2005), Series evaluation of Tweedie exponential
     dispersion model densities. Statistics and Computing 15 (2005): 267-280.
- [3] E. M. Wright (1935), The asymptotic expansion of the generalized Bessel
     function. Proc. London Math. Soc. (2) 38, pp. 257-270.
     https://doi.org/10.1112/plms/s2-38.1.257
- [4] R. B. Paris (2017), The asymptotics of the generalised Bessel function,
     Mathematica Aeterna, Vol. 7, 2017, no. 4, 381 - 406,
     https://arxiv.org/abs/1711.03006
- [5] Y. F. Luchko (2008), Algorithms for Evaluation of the Wright Function for
     the Real Arguments' Values, Fractional Calculus and Applied Analysis 11(1)
     http://sci-gems.math.bas.bg/jspui/bitstream/10525/1298/1/fcaa-vol11-num1-2008-57p-75p.pdf

title: MAINT: linalg: improve input shape consistency checks
body:
#### Reference issue
https://github.com/scipy/scipy/issues/24148#issuecomment-5284580100

#### What does this implement/fix?
Previously, the `_apply_over_batch` would only validate input shapes if an input had zero size.
This changes it to perform the input validation on all input.

For instance, `solve_sylvester(np.eye(2), np.eye(3), np.eye(2))` raises the following in `main`:

```
ValueError: shapes (2,2) and (3,3) not aligned:
2 (dim 1) != 3 (dim 0)
```

With this PR:
```
ValueError: The core shape(s) of the array argument(s):
a: (2, 2), b: (3, 3), q: (2, 2)
is/are incompatible with the shapes in the signature:
a: (i, i), b: (j, j), q: (i, j)
```
Of course, we could add additional logic to make the error as specific as we like.

Even if functions had readable error messages to begin with, this makes the messages consistent so users only have to learn to interpret one type of message. As an added benefit, we could now delete a ton of of function-specific input validation code.

The PR also explains NEP 5 signatures in the `linalg` batch tutorial and fixes some bugs.

#### Additional information 
If we don't want to turn this on for all functions, we can add an option to `_apply_over_batch` to opt in to the input validation. In any case, there's a lot of other little improvements in this PR.

title: BUG: cluster.hierarchy.fcluster: reject t < 1 for maxclust criteria
body:
#### Reference issue

Closes gh-21206.

#### What does this implement/fix?

`fcluster` with `criterion="maxclust"` and `t=0` gives a different answer depending on what
is in memory , instead of complaining .

`cluster_maxclust_monocrit` ends with `MC[upper_idx]` , but `MC` only holds `n-1` values ,
so the last legal index is `n-2` . `upper_idx` starts at `n-1` and only comes down when a
threshold gives few enough clusters . testing `i = n-2` always puts the whole tree into one
cluster , so that test only fails when `max_nc < 1` . in that one case `upper_idx` is never
lowered and `MC[n-1]` is read one past the end of the array .

`_hierarchy.pyx` is compiled with `boundscheck=False` , so nothing catches it and the cutoff
is whatever happens to sit in that memory . with `t=0` on six points the result is six
singleton clusters . passing an `MC` one slot longer with a known value in slot `n-1` changes
the answer , which is what showed where it was reading from .

no `t` can ever produce fewer than one cluster , so the input is rejected instead . that
removes the only path that reaches the read rather than hiding it . `t >= 1` is unchanged ,
and `distance` and `inconsistent` still take `t=0` .

#### Additional information

`t=0.5` is rejected too , it truncated to zero and reached the same line . `t=1.5` still
works .

six new cases cover `maxclust` and `maxclust_monocrit` for `t` of 0 , -1 and 0.5 . they fail
on main with "DID NOT RAISE ValueError" . `pytest scipy/cluster/` gives 225 passed , 6
skipped .

title: BUG: sparse.csgraph: handle duplicate CSR entries in bipartite matching
body:
#### Reference issue

Closes gh-26160

#### What does this implement/fix?

`maximum_bipartite_matching`, `structural_rank` and
`min_weight_full_bipartite_matching` crash (or hang, or return garbage) when the CSR input stores the same entry more than once. `_hopcroft_karp` in `scipy/sparse/csgraph/_matching.pyx` pushes `y[u]` onto a fixed-size DFS stack once for every stored entry that passes the level check, so a row stored `K` times pushes the same row `K` times. The stack has only `i + 1` slots and the extension is compiled with `boundscheck(False)`, so the extra pushes overwrite heap memory.

CSR arrays may legitimately contain duplicate entries — `tocsr()` does not always merge them, and `eliminate_zeros()` / `.T.tocsr()` keep them. A `coo` input is not affected because converting to CSR merges duplicates.

**Changes**

- `scipy/sparse/csgraph/_matching.pyx`:
  - `maximum_bipartite_matching`: merge duplicate entries (copy + `sum_duplicates`) when the input has no canonical format, before calling `_hopcroft_karp`.
  - `min_weight_full_bipartite_matching`: same normalization, before the feasibility search and `_lapjvsp`. Duplicate weights are summed, matching scipy's standard semantics for duplicates.
- `structural_rank` (in `_reordering.pyx`) delegates to `maximum_bipartite_matching`, so it is covered automatically.
- Tests added in `scipy/sparse/csgraph/tests/test_matching.py` for all three functions using `K = 100_000` duplicate entries, which overflow the stack on every platform before this fix.

**Why this approach**

Canonicalizing the input keeps the documented space complexity of `_hopcroft_karp` ($O(|E| \sqrt{|V|})$ time, linear in the number of rows) and also protects `_lapjvsp` (which reads the same arrays in `min_weight_full_bipartite_matching`); growing the stack to `nnz + 1` would break the space guarantee and leave `_lapjvsp` exposed.

#### Verification

- Pre-fix behavior of the issue's reproducer on SciPy 1.18.1 (Python 3.14, Linux):
  - `maximum_bipartite_matching`: **segmentation fault** (exit 139)
  - `structural_rank`: **hang** (no completion within 20 s)
  - `min_weight_full_bipartite_matching`: **segmentation fault** (exit 139)
- Post-fix: same input is normalized to a canonical 3-entry CSR, and the searches return the correct maximum matching (both partitions), structural rank 2, and a valid full matching M-bM-^@M-^T verified on the compiled extension by canonicalizing before the search, mirroring exactly what the added two-line wrappers do.
- The edited `_matching.pyx` passes a full Cython compile.
- Full from-source build (meson + OpenBLAS, Cython 3.3.0) of the branch: `test_matching.py` 37 passed; `scipy/sparse/csgraph/tests/` 1350 passed, 58 skipped; CSR/CSC ABI smoke 37 passed, 1 skipped.

The pre-fix and patched `_matching.pyx` variants were each compiled with Cython and hot-swapped in place, so the crash signatures above come from the real compiled extension rather than an emulation. Review responses are in the thread above.

title: TST: linalg: fix Pyodide hang and crash in wrapper GC tests
body:
#### Reference issue
Closes gh-26266.

#### What does this implement/fix?
Test-only changes in `scipy/linalg/tests/` that stop the Pyodide job from hanging and crashing:

1. **Skip `test_wrapper_module_collected` on WASM** (`test_lapack.py`). This test loads a second, fresh copy of the `_fblas`/`_flapack` extension module. On Pyodide it sometimes hangs until the 45-minute job timeout cancels the run. The last 4 cancelled Emscripten/Pyodide runs all stopped at this test (details in gh-26266). This follows the approach agreed in gh-25713: skip the test so CI stops hanging, and look into the root cause separately.

2. **Use `gc.get_referents` in `test_wrapper_traverses_its_type`** (`test_lapack.py` and `test_blas.py`). With the first test skipped, the [next Pyodide run](https://github.com/scipy/scipy/actions/runs/36097918127/job/107954087650?pr=26267) got further and then crashed on this test with a fatal `RuntimeError: null function or function signature mismatch`. The test used `gc.get_referrers(type(func))`, which calls `tp_traverse` on *every* GC-tracked object in the interpreter. WASM checks function-pointer signatures strictly, so an unrelated extension type loaded earlier in that pytest-split group took the whole process down. The wrapper's own `tp_traverse` signature is correct. The test now checks that `type(func)` is in `gc.get_referents(func)`, which calls only the wrapper's traverse. That is the property under test, and it still fails if the wrapper stops reporting its type. This test keeps running on WASM. `test_blas.py` had the same pattern and got the same change.

3. **Skip `test_self_referential_sequence_raises_recursion_error` on WASM** (`test_blas_lapack_wrappers.py`, added in gh-26243). After the rebase, the [Pyodide run](https://github.com/scipy/scipy/actions/runs/36124404096/job/108037222803) crashed on this test with a fatal `RangeError: Maximum call stack size exceeded`. The test passes a self-referential list as a scalar argument and expects `RecursionError`. On Pyodide the WASM stack runs out before the interpreter's recursion limit is reached, and that is fatal for the whole pytest-split group. The test still runs on all other platforms.

#### Additional information
The hang in (1) is intermittent, so a single green Pyodide run on this PR doesn't prove that fix. `test_wrapper_module_collected` still runs on all other platforms.

The crash in (2) suggests some other extension type has a `tp_traverse` whose signature doesn't match. Finding it would need a debug Pyodide build to map the wasm frames to function names, so I've left that out of this PR.

title: BUG: stats.mannwhitneyu: reduce float32 error in the U statistic
body:
#### Reference issue
Closes gh-24777.

#### What does this implement/fix?
Following up on the discussion in gh-24777: rather than upcasting, compute the statistic more
favourably at the same precision.

`U1` was formed as `R1 - n1*(n1+1)/2`. `R1` is much larger than `U1`, so in float32 it is
accumulated where the representable values are further apart, and the subtraction carries
that coarseness into the result. In the example from the issue, `R1` is about 2.4e7, where
float32 spacing is 2.0, while `U1` is about 6.1e6, where it is 0.5.

This subtracts `(n1 + 1)/2` from each rank before summing, which is algebraically the same
but keeps the accumulation at the magnitude of `U1`. For the example in the issue, the float32
statistic is now `6091893.5`, matching float64, instead of `6091892.0`. The result dtype is
unchanged.

`n1` comes from `_count_nonmasked`, so it is a Python `int` for regular arrays and a per-slice
`MArray` for masked input, where slices can have different counts. The offset is built with
`xp.asarray(..., dtype=ranks.dtype)` so both cases work without promoting the ranks, and it
is broadcast against the last axis. The existing `test_marray.py::test_mannwhitneyu` already
masks elements so that slices have different counts, and it still passes.

#### Additional information
Limitation: this removes the error from accumulating and then cancelling. It can't help when
`U` itself is too large for float32 to represent closely; for example with `n1 = n2 = 50000`
the statistic is around 1.25e9, where float32 spacing is 128.

Tests run locally with `SCIPY_ARRAY_API=1`: `test_hypotests.py`, `test_marray.py`,
`test_stats.py`, `test_axis_nan_policy.py`, all passing. The new test fails on `main` and
passes with this change.

Turns out we're getting better coverage just with randomness, and parametrizing over `shape_options` gives us more control to add specific cases.

<details>

# Shape and broadcasting coverage: `main.npz` versus `PR2.npz`

## Executive summary

`PR2.npz` is much more effective at generating distinct, nontrivial broadcasting configurations within ranks 0 through 3. Despite containing five fewer records, it has 1,543 distinct exact configurations, compared with 888 in `main.npz`. It also uses scalars less often and makes two or more operands broadcast in 93.2% of records, compared with 74.4% in `main.npz`.

`main.npz` has one important advantage: it covers higher dimensionality. Its results reach rank 6, whereas every result in `PR2.npz` has rank at most 3. Consequently, `main.npz` has a larger raw vocabulary of shapes, but much of that advantage comes from ranks 4 through 6 rather than denser coverage at ordinary ranks.

The strongest combined strategy would use PR2-style generation for ranks 0 through 3 and retain a small, deliberate set of rank-4 through rank-6 cases.

## Data and methodology

Each record was normalized to

```text
(tuple(parameter_shapes), x_shape, y_shape)
```

NumPy integer dimensions were converted to Python integers before comparisons. All parameter shapes, the `x` shape, and the `y` shape were treated as separate broadcasting operands. The broadcast-result shape was computed with `numpy.broadcast_shapes`.

The archives contain only shape information. They do not identify the distribution or operation associated with each record. Therefore, two records with the same shapes may still test different implementations. Counts of duplicates in this report measure duplication of shape configurations, not necessarily redundant tests.

## Definitions

The short labels used below have the following precise meanings.

**Exact configuration**

The complete ordered combination of all parameter shapes, the `x` shape, and the `y` shape. Parameter order is significant. Two records are exact duplicates only when all these shapes agree.

**Structural broadcast pattern**

A configuration after discarding the particular values of ordinary dimensions while retaining:

- the number of parameter operands;
- every operand's rank;
- operand order;
- on every aligned axis, whether each operand has a missing leading axis, dimension zero, dimension one, or an ordinary dimension greater than one.

Thus, structurally equivalent examples such as `(2, 1)` with `(1, 3)` and `(4, 1)` with `(1, 2)` count as the same pattern. Zero is kept distinct because zero-length broadcasting has special behavior.

**Implicit leading-axis expansion** or **rank padding**

At least one operand has fewer axes than the broadcast result. NumPy aligns shapes from the right, which is equivalent to prepending dimensions of size one to the shorter operand. A scalar broadcasting to any nonscalar result is included in this category.

**Mixed operand ranks**

Not all operands have the same rank. For these mutually broadcastable records, this is equivalent to saying that at least one operand undergoes implicit leading-axis expansion.

**Singleton expansion**

At least one explicit input dimension of size one aligns with a result dimension that is not one. This includes both ordinary cases such as `1 -> 4` and zero-length cases such as `1 -> 0`. Merely prepending an implicit dimension to a shorter operand does not by itself count as singleton expansion.

**No broadcasting required**

Every operand shape is already exactly equal to the result shape. This is stricter than merely saying that the shapes are mutually broadcastable. For example, `()` with `(3,)` does require broadcasting under this definition.

**Operand changed to the result shape**

An operand's original shape is not exactly equal to the broadcast-result shape. This includes changes caused by rank padding, singleton expansion, or both. It describes logical shape expansion; it does not imply that NumPy materializes a copied array.

**Zero-length dimension present**

At least one operand has an explicit dimension of size zero. Because every record is mutually broadcastable, the corresponding result axis is also zero-length.

**Zero against singleton**

On at least one aligned axis, one operand has an explicit zero and another has an explicit one. Missing leading axes do not count as explicit singleton dimensions for this metric. For example, `(0, 3)` with `(1, 3)` qualifies and broadcasts to `(0, 3)`.

**Same-rank, multidirectional singleton expansion**

At least two nonscalar operands have the same rank as the result and expand explicit singleton dimensions on different axes. For example, `(3, 1)` with `(1, 4)` broadcasts to `(3, 4)`: the first operand expands on the second axis and the second operand expands on the first.

**Three operands owning different result axes**

At least three distinct operands uniquely provide ordinary dimensions greater than one on three distinct result axes. On each such axis, the other operands have either a singleton dimension or a missing leading axis. A canonical example is `(2, 1, 1)`, `(1, 3, 1)`, and `(1, 1, 4)`, which broadcast to `(2, 3, 4)`.

**All operands scalar**

Every parameter shape, the `x` shape, and the `y` shape is `()`.

## Overall diversity

| Metric | `main.npz` | `PR2.npz` |
|---|---:|---:|
| Records | 2,025 | 2,020 |
| Distinct exact configurations | 888 (43.9%) | 1,543 (76.4%) |
| Repeated records by exact shape | 1,137 | 477 |
| Largest multiplicity of one exact configuration | 232 | 49 |
| Distinct structural broadcast patterns | 877 | 1,223 |
| Distinct input shapes across all roles | 269 | 155 |
| Distinct broadcast-result shapes | 273 | 156 |

PR2 produces 655 more distinct exact configurations with five fewer records. Its lower raw count of distinct shapes is explained by its rank cap: PR2 draws from a compact rank-0-through-rank-3 universe, while main reaches rank 6.

The most common exact configuration in both archives is the one-parameter all-scalar case:

```text
parameter shapes = [()], x = (), y = () -> result = ()
```

It occurs 232 times in main and 49 times in PR2.

## Rank coverage

### Broadcast-result ranks

| Result rank | `main.npz` | `PR2.npz` |
|---:|---:|---:|
| 0 | 448 (22.1%) | 69 (3.4%) |
| 1 | 315 (15.6%) | 301 (14.9%) |
| 2 | 659 (32.5%) | 619 (30.6%) |
| 3 | 223 (11.0%) | 1,031 (51.0%) |
| 4 | 298 (14.7%) | 0 |
| 5 | 42 (2.1%) | 0 |
| 6 | 40 (2.0%) | 0 |

Main assigns 18.8% of its records to result ranks 4 through 6. PR2 instead concentrates just over half of its records at rank 3.

### Distinct input shapes by rank

| Input-shape rank | `main.npz` | `PR2.npz` | Possible in PR2's `{0,1,2,3,4}` dimension universe |
|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| 0 | 1 | 1 | 1 |
| 1 | 5 | 5 | 5 |
| 2 | 21 | 25 | 25 |
| 3 | 60 | 124 | 125 |
| 4 | 110 | 0 | Not in scope |
| 5 | 34 | 0 | Not in scope |
| 6 | 38 | 0 | Not in scope |

PR2 covers every possible rank-0, rank-1, and rank-2 input shape using dimensions `{0,1,2,3,4}`. At rank 3 it covers 124 of 125 possibilities; the only absent input shape is `(2, 2, 0)`. That shape does occur as a broadcast result, so PR2 still covers all 156 possible result shapes in its bounded universe.

## Coverage by operand role

| Role | Metric | `main.npz` | `PR2.npz` |
|---|---|---:|---:|
| Parameters | Operand occurrences | 3,370 | 3,360 |
| Parameters | Distinct shapes | 13 | 148 |
| Parameters | Scalar occurrences | 1,921 (57.0%) | 1,426 (42.4%) |
| `x` | Operand occurrences | 2,025 | 2,020 |
| `x` | Distinct shapes | 143 | 139 |
| `x` | Scalar occurrences | 929 (45.9%) | 539 (26.7%) |
| `y` | Operand occurrences | 2,025 | 2,020 |
| `y` | Distinct shapes | 219 | 115 |
| `y` | Scalar occurrences | 1,042 (51.5%) | 558 (27.6%) |

The most substantial PR2 improvement is parameter-shape diversity: 148 distinct shapes rather than 13. Main's larger `y` vocabulary is primarily a consequence of permitting ranks 4 through 6.

Across all roles, 52.5% of main's operands are scalar, compared with 34.1% of PR2's operands.

## Broadcasting mechanisms

| Per-record condition | `main.npz` | `PR2.npz` |
|---|---:|---:|
| No broadcasting required | 453 (22.4%) | 76 (3.8%) |
| Implicit leading-axis expansion, without singleton expansion | 872 (43.1%) | 750 (37.1%) |
| Singleton expansion, without implicit leading-axis expansion | 2 (0.1%) | 46 (2.3%) |
| Both mechanisms | 698 (34.5%) | 1,148 (56.8%) |
| Any implicit leading-axis expansion | 1,570 (77.5%) | 1,898 (94.0%) |
| Any singleton expansion | 700 (34.6%) | 1,194 (59.1%) |
| Zero-length dimension present | 728 (36.0%) | 705 (34.9%) |

The four mechanism rows at the top of the table are mutually exclusive and exhaust all records. PR2's main improvement is not merely that it broadcasts more often: it combines rank padding and explicit singleton expansion in 56.8% of records, compared with 34.5% in main.

### Number of operands changed to the result shape

| Changed operands | `main.npz` | `PR2.npz` |
|---:|---:|---:|
| 0 | 453 (22.4%) | 76 (3.8%) |
| 1 | 65 (3.2%) | 61 (3.0%) |
| 2 | 451 (22.3%) | 711 (35.2%) |
| 3 | 749 (37.0%) | 798 (39.5%) |
| 4 | 307 (15.2%) | 374 (18.5%) |

Records have either three operands (one parameter, `x`, and `y`) or four operands (two parameters, `x`, and `y`). PR2 changes at least two operands in 1,883 records, or 93.2% of the archive. Main does so in 1,507 records, or 74.4%.

## Selected situations

| Situation | `main.npz` | `PR2.npz` |
|---|---:|---:|
| Same-rank, multidirectional singleton expansion | 12 | 38 |
| Three operands owning different result axes | 3 | 2 |
| Zero against singleton | 359 | 399 |
| All operands scalar | 448 | 69 |

Both archives contain every selected situation. PR2 gives substantially more coverage to same-rank multidirectional expansion and slightly more to explicit zero-versus-singleton broadcasting. Cases in which three operands independently determine three result axes remain rare in both archives.

The all-scalar count is large in main because it includes records associated with different parameter counts and, potentially, different distributions. It should not automatically be interpreted as 448 redundant tests. As shape coverage alone, however, it is heavy repetition of the same baseline condition.

## Dimension values

Counting every explicit axis in every operand:

| Dimension value | `main.npz` | `PR2.npz` |
|---:|---:|---:|
| 0 | 1,273 | 1,168 |
| 1 | 4,221 | 4,730 |
| 2 | 1,122 | 1,213 |
| 3 | 304 | 1,270 |
| 4 | 89 | 1,254 |
| 5 | 8 | 0 |

On non-singleton ordinary dimensions, PR2 is much more balanced across sizes 2, 3, and 4. Main is strongly concentrated on size 2 and uses size 5 only eight times. The high frequency of ones in both archives is expected for generators designed to produce mutually broadcastable shapes.

## Assessment

Within ranks 0 through 3, PR2 is the stronger suite by a wide margin. It provides:

- many more exact and structural configurations;
- nearly exhaustive coverage of its intended input-shape universe;
- dramatically broader parameter-shape coverage;
- fewer all-scalar and otherwise non-broadcasting records;
- more cases combining rank padding with explicit singleton expansion; and
- more cases in which several operands change shape simultaneously.

Main remains valuable for a separate reason: high-rank coverage. It has 380 records whose broadcast result has rank 4, 5, or 6, including 82 at ranks 5 and 6. PR2 tests none of these ranks.

If PR2 is intended to replace main entirely, loss of high-rank coverage is the principal regression. If high-rank behavior is not inherently important, PR2 is a clear improvement. If it is important, a compact deterministic supplement of representative rank-4-through-rank-6 configurations would preserve main's distinctive benefit without restoring its heavy scalar duplication.

body:
#### Reference issue
Closes gh-3588.

#### What does this implement/fix?
Three test modules (`cluster/hierarchy/tests/test_hierarchy.py`, `spatial/tests/test__plotutils.py` and `stats/tests/test_morestats.py`) set matplotlib's backend to Agg at import time. So after running the tests in a session the process is left on Agg and the user's plots stop showing up, which is what gh-3588 describes.

I went with the fixture pv suggested on the issue: `mpl_agg` in `scipy/conftest.py` switches to Agg for a plotting test, closes the figures and switches back afterwards. One thing to be aware of: the fixture restores whatever backend was resolved before the test. Matplotlib doesn't offer a public way back to the unresolved "auto" state. I checked this in-process with `pytest.main` on headless Linux (matplotlib 3.11.2). I don't have a machine with a GUI toolkit, so if someone with a display could run the plotting tests with `MPLBACKEND` unset and check `matplotlib.get_backend()` afterwards, that would be really helpful.

title: BUG: stats.yeojohnson: return lmbda=1 for arbitrary constant inputs
body:
#### Description

This PR fixes an issue in `scipy.stats.yeojohnson_normmax` where passing a constant 1D array results in arbitrary and extreme optimal λ values.

When applying the Yeo-Johnson transform to constant data, the variance is zero regardless of the λ applied. Because the log-likelihood calculation includes the logarithm of the variance, that part of the equation evaluates to negative infinity (making the likelihood undefined) for any λ. The optimizer ends up chasing floating-point rounding errors during these operations, leading to silent numerical explosions. For example:

* Constant `4` →λ≈76.7, transformed values ≈ `5e51`
* Constant `1000` → transformed values ≈ `3e100`
* Constant `-3` →λ≈−43.5

To resolve this safely, this PR generalizes the existing fallback mechanism. Previously, `yeojohnson_normmax` explicitly checked for arrays of all zeros and returned λ=1. This check has now been broadened to apply to any constant array.

Returning λ=1 is the safest default, as it reduces the transform to the identity function, leaving the constant inputs unchanged. While the sibling function `boxcox` raises an error on constant data, SciPy already has backward-compatibility tests relying on `yeojohnson_normmax([0, 0, 0])` returning a finite value. Expanding this fallback fixes the bug without introducing breaking changes.

(Note for maintainers: If the preference is to align strictly with `boxcox` and raise a `ValueError` for all constant arrays, including zeros, I am happy to update the PR).

#### Modifications & Testing

* Updated `yeojohnson_normmax` to check for equality against the first element instead of zero.
* Verified that `nan_policy='omit'` works seamlessly: since NaNs are already stripped before the constant check, constant arrays with NaNs naturally return λ=1 without requiring extra logic.
* Added parameterized tests for `yeojohnson` and `yeojohnson_normmax` covering various constants (`-3`, `0.001`, `1`, `4`, `1000`).
* Added tests asserting that the transformed array is identical to the input array (tested on cases without NaNs).
* Added a test verifying that λ=1 is correctly returned for a constant input containing a NaN.

The rough idea behind the batching is touched on in https://discuss.scientific-python.org/t/batching-linearoperator-status-and-benchmarks/2199 — we iterate through the entire batch until every system has converged (or we hit `maxiter` etc.). We mask out converged systems in some places to try to avoid too much superfluous computation or divergence-after-convergence. This is expected to yield benefits for large batches of systems where vectorising the `matvec` function is efficient and each system in the batch takes a similar amount of iterations to converge. It is assumed to not do much better than serial calls when a vectorised matvec is not much faster, for small batches, or when a single system can take many more iterations than another in the batch.

My plan is to go back to the forum with benchmarking results once we are happy that the implementation and tests look solid here. https://github.com/scipy/scipy/pull/24745#issuecomment-4075915712 shows promise for at least one problem vs batched dense solvers, with significant memory benefits and performance benefits for large batches of small-to-medium matrices. https://discuss.scientific-python.org/t/batching-linearoperator-status-and-benchmarks/2199 shows promise for large batches of smaller batched sparse and dense systems vs using the existing `cg` serially.

title: BUG: optimize: initialise iterations before the early exits
body:
#### Reference issue

Closes gh-25955.

#### What does this implement/fix?

`bisect`, `ridder`, `brentq` and `brenth` set `solver_stats->iterations` only *after* the checks for an endpoint being a root and for the bracket not changing sign. Those exits return with the field never written, so `root_scalar` reports whatever the struct happened to hold.

The initialisation moves next to `error_num = INPROGRESS`, so it is set on every path out of the function.

#### Additional information

The issue reports wild values. What I see on 1.18.0 is worse in a quieter way — a plausible small count left behind by an earlier call. Running an interior root first, then an endpoint root, makes it deterministic:

```python
from scipy import optimize
def f(x): return x**3 - 1

for m in ['brentq', 'brenth', 'bisect', 'ridder', 'toms748']:
    interior = optimize.root_scalar(f, bracket=(0.5, 10.0), method=m).iterations
    endpoint = optimize.root_scalar(f, bracket=(1.0, 10.0), method=m).iterations
    print(f"{m:8s} interior={interior:3d}  endpoint={endpoint:3d}")
```

```
brentq   interior= 11  endpoint=  6
brenth   interior= 10  endpoint=  6
bisect   interior= 43  endpoint=  6
ridder   interior=  9  endpoint=  6
toms748  interior=  6  endpoint=  0
```

All four report `6`, which is `toms748`'s count from the previous loop iteration — a different solver's leftover. `toms748` is pure Python and already reports 0.

I do not have a Fortran toolchain here, so rather than guess I compiled the four files in `scipy/optimize/Zeros/` standalone against `zeros.h` and called them directly, with the stats struct filled with `0xAB` beforehand:

```

before, endpoint root  -1414812757  (same)  (same)  (same)
after,  endpoint root            0       0       0       0
before, interior root           11      10      43       9
after,  interior root           11      10      43       9
```

So the counts for brackets that actually iterate are untouched; only the early exits change. The `SIGNERR` exit is covered by the same move.

`test_gh_25955_iterations_when_endpoint_is_root` in `scipy/optimize/tests/test_zeros.py`, parametrised over `bracket_methods` and over which endpoint is the root. It runs an iterating bracket first so a stale count is present to be read.

I could not run scipy's own suite locally for the reason above, so I ran the test body against released 1.18.0 to confirm it distinguishes the two states: **8 of 10 parameter combinations fail**, and the two `toms748` cases pass, which is the expected split.

title: BUG: initialize bracketing solver iteration counts
body:
#### Reference issue
Closes gh-25955.

#### What does this implement/fix?
`bisect`, `brentq`, `brenth`, and `ridder` (the C bracketing solvers backing
`scipy.optimize.root_scalar`) returned as soon as they detected that one
bracket endpoint was already a root, but `solver_stats->iterations` was only
initialized to 0 *after* that early-return check, inside the main iteration
loop. When a bracket endpoint was itself the root, the function returned
before that initialization ran, so `iterations` was left holding whatever
value happened to be in that stack memory, and Python-level callers using
`full_output=True` could observe an uninitialized/garbage iteration count for
an otherwise valid, zero-iteration result.

This moves `solver_stats->iterations = 0` up to just after `error_num` is set
at the top of each function, before the endpoint checks, so it is always
initialized regardless of which return path is taken. The iteration-counting
logic in the main loop is unchanged. `toms748` was not touched because it
already initializes/returns zero iterations correctly in this case.

over `brentq`, `brenth`, `bisect`, and `ridder`, and over which bracket
endpoint (0 or 1) is the root, asserting the correct root is returned and

title: BUG: handle single coefficient in cspline1d_eval/qspline1d_eval
body:
#### Reference issue
Closes gh-25090.

#### What does this implement/fix?
`cspline1d_eval` and `qspline1d_eval` evaluate a spline outside its knot
range `[0, N-1]` (where `N = len(cj)`) using mirror-symmetric recursion to
fold the query point back into range. When the coefficient array has only
one element (`N == 1`), that range degenerates to a single point `[0, 0]`,
so the mirror never folds the point back in range and the recursion never
terminates, raising `RecursionError`.

For a single coefficient the spline is constant at every coordinate, so this
adds a special case that fills the result with that coefficient and returns
directly, bypassing the recursive mirroring for `N == 1`. This matches what
the general (non-mirrored) evaluation formula already produces at `N == 1`
via the B-spline basis functions' partition-of-unity property, so it does
not change the function's existing semantics for any other input.

While diagnosing the issue in `cspline1d_eval`, I found the identical
mirror-recursion structure, and therefore the identical `RecursionError` bug,
in the sibling function `qspline1d_eval` (not covered by the original issue
report). Since both functions share the same underlying defect, this PR
fixes both.

#### Additional information
Added regression tests to `scipy/signal/tests/test_bsplines.py` for both
`cspline1d_eval` and `qspline1d_eval`, evaluating a single-coefficient spline
at negative, zero, and positive coordinates.

Verified locally against a wheel built from this branch:

**Root cause:** The mirror-symmetry recursion reflects negative points to positive (`-newx`), but with N=1 the positive point exceeds N-1=0, triggering the other reflection (`2*(N-1) - newx = -newx`), bouncing back to negative indefinitely.

**Fix:** For N=1, the spline is a constant function (the single coefficient value everywhere) under mirror-symmetric boundary conditions. Return `cj[0]` early. Applied to both `cspline1d_eval` and `qspline1d_eval`.

```python
>>> from scipy.signal import cspline1d_eval
>>> cspline1d_eval(np.array([1.0]), np.array([-0.1]))  # Before: RecursionError
array([1.])  # After: correct
```

Closes #25090.

title: ENH: interpolate.make_smoothing_spline: support GCV algorithm for user defined knots
body:
#### Reference issue
Part 2 of gh-25862. That PR added support for user-provided knots `t` with an explicit `lam`, this one adds automatic `lam` selection via GCV, so `lam=None` works for user knots the same way it does for the default knots.

#### What does this implement/fix?
This PR adapts the Generalized Cross Validation algorithm for the case when user passes the knot vector. The previous GCV path assumed that knots are always at the data sites. This PR implements the general case of the GCV algorithm
implementing the formulas defined in [this](https://github.com/aadya940/scipy-bspline-testing/blob/main/B_Splines_with_arbitary_knots-gcv.pdf) companion report Section 12.

#### Additional information

**Design**
- The search is scale-free. We compute the scale `r = tr(XᵀWX) / tr(Ω)` and minimize the GCV criterion over `s = log10(lam / r)` in a fixed bounded window, instead of searching `lam` directly.
- Rescaling `x` or `y` rescales the selected `lam` by exactly the right factor and returns the same spline.
- The window edges match the two failure extremes of the linear system: below it the penalty is under the roundoff of the data term, above it the system is numerically singular. This also avoids the failures of linear-scale search discussed in gh-23472.

**Implementation**
- The influence-matrix trace is computed from the banded Cholesky factor using de Hoog's formula, so each evaluation of the criterion is `O(m)`. No dense inverse is formed.
- Upper-banded (LAPACK) storage is used throughout the user-knots path.
- Solver failures inside the search propagate as `LinAlgError`.
- TODO left in the code: estimate the condition number via LAPACK `dpbcon` once it is wrapped in `scipy.linalg` (separate follow-up PR later).

**Tests**
- Main test: knots at all data sites must reproduce the default GCV path.
- Grid-argmin check of the GCV criterion.
- Auto-selection compared against R's `smooth.spline` with forced knots.
- Weighted data.
- Scale-invariance at scales from `3e-6` to `1e6`.

It compares the expected mathematical or semantic result with the current source behavior. Private decorated helpers are represented by their public functions. Python and Cython sources/templates are included. The inventory contains 61 public APIs, expanded to 85 signature/variant entries. A signature below is the signature currently declared in the source, unless it is explicitly marked as inferred. ## Potentially nonzero-size cases: current behavior is appropriate
pinvh(..., return_rank=True): (i,j)->(i,j),int() The current result has an empty pseudoinverse and scalar rank `0`, as it should. `pinvh` is square in its documented domain, so the matrix shape is not problematic here.
eigvalsh_tridiagonal(d, e): (i),(j)->(i) The valid case `i=1,j=0` is handled by the implementation and returns the sole diagonal value `d[0]`. Empty zero-by-zero cases return an empty array.
eigh_tridiagonal(..., eigvals_only=True): (i),(j)->(i,) For `i=1,j=0`, the current implementation returns `d[0]`, as expected; for the empty zero-by-zero case it returns an empty eigenvalue array.
eigh_tridiagonal(..., eigvals_only=False): (i),(j)->(i,),(i,i) For `i=1,j=0`, the current implementation returns the sole eigenvalue and a one-by-one eigenvector, equivalent to the identity up to normalization. Empty zero-by-zero inputs return empty factors.
polar(..., side='right'): (i,j)->(i,j),(j,j) For `i=0,j>0`, the current zero-size result has empty `U` and an all-zero `j`-by-`j` `P`, which is the canonical positive-semidefinite factor of the zero matrix.
polar(..., side='left'): (i,j)->(i,j),(i,i) For `j=0,i>0`, the current result has empty `U` and an all-zero `i`-by-`i` `P`, as expected.
qr_multiply(..., pivoting=True, ...): inferred QR/product shapes plus pivot vector The decorator has no explicit signature. For a zero-row input with `j>0`, the current empty-QR path returns an identity permutation of length `j`; the other returned factors are empty. This is a natural and valid pivot result.
qr_delete(..., which='row', N=0, M>p>0, ...): inferred QR-factor shapes For a full QR factorization of an `M`-by-zero matrix, deleting `p` rows should return a nonempty orthogonal `Q1` of shape `(M-p,M-p)` and an empty `R1`. The current source follows this factor-shape logic, so the result is consistent with the expected decomposition.
qr_insert(..., which='row', M=0, N>0, p>0, ...): inferred QR-factor shapes Inserting `p` rows into the full factors of a zero-row, `N`-column matrix should produce `Q1` with shape `(p,p)` and `R1` with shape `(p,N)`. The current source constructs those factors, including the identity-like new orthogonal block, so this case is appropriate.
qr_insert(..., which='col', M>0, N=0, p>0, ...): inferred QR-factor shapes Inserting `p` columns into the full factors of an `M`-row, zero-column matrix should produce nonempty updated factors when `M,p>0`. The current source supports this shape transition, so the result is consistent with the expected decomposition.
rq(..., mode='full', ...): (i,j)->(i,j),(j,j) For `i=0,j>0`, the current empty-array path returns empty `R` and `Q=eye(j)`. That is a valid full RQ decomposition of the empty matrix.
schur(..., sort=...,): (i,i)->(i,i),(i,i),() For an empty matrix with sorting requested, the current result contains empty `T` and `Z` and scalar `sdim=0`, which is correct.
null_space(A): (m,n)->(n,n) For `A.shape==(0,n)`, the whole `n`-dimensional domain is the null space. The current SVD path returns an orthonormal basis of that space, conventionally the identity. For `n=0`, it returns an empty basis.
subspace_angles(...): (i,j),(i,k)->float(min(j,k),) For `i=0,j,k>0`, the requested positive number of principal angles is undefined because both column spaces collapse to the zero subspace. The current result is a NaN array of shape `(min(j,k),)`, which is an appropriate way to preserve the declared output shape without inventing angles.
expm_cond(A): (i,i)->float() The empty case reduces the relative condition-number expression to zero over zero. The current result is `NaN`, which correctly reports that the condition number is undefined.
orthogonal_procrustes(A, B): (i,j),(i,j)->(j,j),float() If either `i=0` or `j=0`, the current implementation returns an orthogonal `R` factor (the identity in the empty-data case) and `scale=0`. The objective contains no data, so any orthogonal `R` is optimal; identity is a valid canonical choice.

#### What does this implement/fix?
<!--Please explain your changes.-->

`linalg.inv` does several optimizations internally, and two of them conspired to a segfault:

title: ENH: stats: Add distance correlation, distance covariance, and energy distance (#13728)
body:
#### Reference issue
Closes #13728

#### What does this implement/fix?
This PR implements **multivariate distance correlation**, **distance covariance**, and **energy distance** in `scipy.stats._distance_correlation`, completely derived from primary literature (Székely et al., 2007; Székely & Rizzo, 2014; Rizzo & Székely, 2016).

Unlike external packages (e.g. `hyppo` or `dcor`), this implementation is **100% pure Python/NumPy/SciPy**, completely free of third-party compilation dependencies (no Numba required), and fully compliant with SciPy's BSD-3 licensing.

#### Key Functions Added:
1. **`distance_covariance(x, y, *, method="auto", metric="euclidean")`**:
   - Computes sample distance covariance $d\text{Cov}_n(X, Y)$ using $O(n^2)$ vectorized double-centering.
   - Non-negative for all samples; equals 0 if and only if $X$ and $Y$ are independent.
   - Supports classical biased estimation and unbiased U-centering estimator (Székely & Rizzo, 2014).
2. **`distance_correlation(x, y, *, method="auto", metric="euclidean")`**:
   - Scale- and dimension-free dependence metric $d\text{Cor}_n(X, Y) \in [0, 1]$.
   - Sensitive to arbitrary non-linear associations (circular, parabolic, sinusoidal, cluster) where Pearson correlation is 0.
3. **`distance_covariance_test(x, y, *, permutations=999, metric="euclidean", workers=1, random_state=None)`**:
   - Nonparametric permutation test of independence returning `DistanceCovarianceResult(statistic, pvalue, null_distribution)`.
   - Optimized permutation engine: pre-computes double-centered distance matrices once; evaluates row-and-column indexed permutations $B_{\pi} = B[\pi, :][:, \pi]$ in $O(n^2)$ without recomputing distances or means.
   - Supports multi-processing via `MapWrapper`.
4. **`energy_distance_nd(u, v, *, metric="euclidean")`**:
   - Multivariate energy distance test statistic for equality of distributions in arbitrary dimensions $\mathbb{R}^d$.

#### Unit Tests:
- Added `scipy/stats/tests/test_distance_correlation.py` with 29 comprehensive unit tests (100% passing) covering input validation, mathematical symmetries, linear invariance, non-linear dependence detection, permutation calibration, and distribution shift detection.
